tagline: A short, carefully told story of famine, loss, and loyal love, in which a Moabite widow becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
overview:
Ruth is a four-chapter story set “in the days when the judges ruled” (1:1), the same dark period as the book of Judges, but told from inside one family in the small town of Bethlehem. A famine drives Elimelech, his wife Naomi, and their two sons across the Jordan to Moab. The men die there. Naomi turns home with nothing, and her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth refuses to leave her, binding herself to Naomi, to her people, and to her God. Back in Bethlehem, Ruth gleans in the fields of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, and through his generosity and a daring night visit to the threshing floor, Boaz becomes the family's redeemer. He marries Ruth, buys back the family land, and a son is born to carry on the dead man's name.

The book ends with a surprise that changes how the whole story reads. The child, Obed, is the grandfather of David, Israel's great king. A story that looked private and small (two widows, a field, a legal hearing at the town gate) turns out to be the hinge between the chaos of the judges and the coming of the monarchy.

Ruth matters for more than its ending. It shows ordinary people living out covenant loyalty (the Hebrew word is hesed, steadfast love that goes beyond what duty requires) in a time when Israel's leaders mostly did not. It shows God at work without a single miracle, through a harvest, a chance turn into the right field, and the choices of faithful people. And it places a foreign woman from a despised nation at the root of Israel's royal line.
author: The book doesn't name its author. The Babylonian Talmud (Bava Batra 14b-15a), a collection of Jewish rabbinic teaching completed around AD 500, records the tradition that Samuel wrote it, along with Judges and his own book. Most scholars today, including many who hold a high view of Scripture, doubt that attribution, mainly because the genealogy reaches David and Samuel died before David became king. Some scholars have suggested that the book's sympathetic focus on women's voices and concerns points to a female author or to stories told among women; others think that goes beyond the evidence. The honest answer is that the writer is unknown, a skilled storyteller who knew Israel's laws, customs, and older traditions well.
date: The story is set in the period of the judges, roughly the twelfth and eleventh centuries BC, but the book was written later: 4:7 explains a custom from “former times in Israel,” and the genealogy ends with David. Beyond that, scholars divide. Many date the book to the monarchy, perhaps in the time of David or Solomon (tenth century BC) or somewhat after, arguing that its interest in David's ancestry makes most sense while the Davidic house was being established, and pointing to features of its Hebrew they take as early. Others date it after the exile, in the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BC), and read it alongside Ezra and Nehemiah, whose reforms forbade marriage to foreign women including Moabites; on this view Ruth offers a gentler counterpoint. Scholars also dispute how much the book's language can settle the question, since some of its apparently late or unusual forms may reflect dialect or deliberate storytelling style. Both positions are held by careful readers.
setting:
The book moves between two places. Bethlehem, in the hill country of Judah about six miles south of Jerusalem, was a farming town whose name means house of bread, which makes the famine of chapter 1 sharply ironic. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, on the high plateau between the Arnon and Zered valleys. Israel's traditions traced the Moabites to Lot's son born of incest (Genesis 19:30-38), remembered Moab's king hiring Balaam to curse Israel and Moabite women drawing Israelites into idolatry (Numbers 22-25), and barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3-6). The chief god of Moab was Chemosh, named in the Bible and on the Mesha Stele, a Moabite royal inscription from the ninth century BC.

The story's daily life is agricultural: the barley harvest in spring (around April) and the wheat harvest that followed into early summer, gleaning rights for the poor, threshing floors, and the town gate where elders settled legal matters. Two institutions from Israel's law stand behind the plot: the duty of a near kinsman to redeem family land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25) and the custom of a brother marrying his dead brother's widow to raise up a son in the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). Ruth doesn't match either law exactly, and how the book relates to them is much discussed.
purpose: Several purposes are visible, and they don't exclude one another. The book traces the ancestry of David and shows that his line rose out of faithful kindness and God's quiet care, not from power. It sets a picture of covenant loyalty against the backdrop of the judges, showing what faithfulness looks like in ordinary life when Israel's public life had collapsed. It shows a foreigner embracing Israel's God and being received into Israel, which spoke to any generation asking who belongs to the people of God. And it treats bitterness and grief honestly: Naomi's complaint against God is not rebuked but answered, slowly, by events. In Jewish practice Ruth is read at Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, which falls at the time of the wheat harvest.
story: In Christian Bibles, following the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), Ruth stands between Judges and 1 Samuel. There it acts as a bridge: Judges closes with the words that everyone did what was right in his own eyes because Israel had no king, and Ruth closes with the name of David, the king to come. 1 Samuel then tells how David's kingdom arrives. In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth belongs to the third section, the Writings, as one of the five short scrolls (the Megillot) read at the festivals; in many printed Hebrew Bibles it follows Proverbs, whose final poem praises a woman of noble character, the same phrase Boaz uses of Ruth (3:11). Either placement shapes how the book is heard. Ruth also looks back to Genesis: its closing blessing recalls Rachel and Leah, the mothers of Israel, and Tamar, another foreign woman whose unconventional action preserved Judah's line (Genesis 38).
christ: The New Testament names Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus: Matthew 1:5 lists Boaz as the father of Obed by Ruth, one of four women (with Tamar, Rahab, and Bathsheba) in that list, several of them foreigners and all with irregular stories. Through Obed, Jesse, and David, the line runs to the one Christians confess as the Son of David. Beyond the genealogy, the book's central idea is redemption by a kinsman: a near relative who has the right and the means to buy back what was lost and to restore a family that had no future. The New Testament uses the same language of Christ, who shares our flesh as a true kinsman (Hebrews 2:14-17) and redeems his people at his own cost. Boaz is not a hidden prediction of Jesus, and the book doesn't present him as one. The link is a pattern that the rest of Scripture fills out: God providing a redeemer from within the family, and gathering outsiders under his wings.
reading: Ruth is a narrative told with great economy and craft, and it rewards slow reading. Watch the dialogue, which carries most of the story, and the key words that come back in new settings: return, empty and full, kindness, rest, wings, and redeem. Notice how the chapters are balanced, with scenes on the road, in the field, at the threshing floor, and at the gate, and how Naomi's emptiness in chapter 1 is answered by the child in her lap in chapter 4. Notice, too, how God acts: he is spoken to and spoken of constantly, but the narrator describes him acting directly only twice (1:6 and 4:13). Common misreadings include treating the book as a simple romance, which misses its concern with land, law, lineage, and loyalty to the dead, and treating the threshing-floor scene as either plainly sexual or plainly innocent when the text is deliberately delicate and suggestive.

structure.title: Emptiness and return
structure.summary: Famine, exile in Moab, and three deaths leave Naomi without husband or sons. She returns to Bethlehem, and Ruth refuses to leave her, pledging herself to Naomi's people and God.

structure.title: Gleaning in the field of Boaz
structure.summary: Ruth gleans in the barley harvest and happens on the field of Boaz, who treats her with unusual generosity. Naomi learns that he is a kinsman-redeemer.

structure.title: The night at the threshing floor
structure.summary: At Naomi's direction Ruth goes to Boaz at night and asks him to spread his garment over her as redeemer. He agrees, but a nearer relative must be given the first right.

structure.title: Redemption at the gate and the birth of Obed
structure.summary: Boaz settles the matter before the elders, the nearer redeemer declines, and Boaz marries Ruth. Their son Obed restores Naomi, and a genealogy leads to David.

themes.title: Hesed: loyal, generous love
themes.body: The Hebrew word hesed names a love that keeps faith within a relationship and goes beyond what duty requires. Naomi prays that the LORD will show it to her daughters-in-law (1:8); Ruth shows it to Naomi and later to Boaz (3:10); Boaz shows it in the field; and Naomi blesses the LORD for not withdrawing it from the living or the dead (2:20). The book suggests that God's own faithfulness often reaches people through the faithfulness of others.

themes.title: Providence without miracles
themes.body: No one in Ruth sees a vision or witnesses a wonder. Famine ends, harvests come, Ruth happens to enter the field of Boaz, the nearer redeemer happens to pass by the gate. The narrator lets the reader see God's hand in these ordinary turns without forcing the point. Ruth is one of the Bible's clearest pictures of a God who governs the small events of ordinary life for his purposes.

themes.title: Redemption and the kinsman-redeemer
themes.body: The go'el, or kinsman-redeemer, was a near relative responsible for protecting a family's land, name, and people when they could not protect themselves. The word and its verb run through chapters 2 to 4. Boaz takes on the role at cost to himself, and the book shows redemption not as an abstraction but as a person acting to restore land, household, and future.

themes.title: The outsider brought in
themes.body: Ruth is repeatedly called the Moabitess, and she calls herself a foreigner. Yet she chooses Israel's God, is sheltered under his wings, and becomes an ancestor of David. The book does not deny Israel's law about Moab, but it shows the door of God's people open to a foreigner who takes refuge in the LORD, a theme the prophets and the New Testament develop.

themes.title: Emptiness turned to fullness
themes.body: Naomi leaves full and returns empty, and she says so bitterly. The book answers her lament not with an argument but with events: grain in Ruth's shawl, a redeemer found, a son placed in her lap. It treats grief and complaint honestly, and lets hope arrive slowly.

keyChapters.why: Ruth's pledge to Naomi (1:16-17) is one of the great statements of loyalty in literature, and Naomi's bitter return sets up the whole book.
The chance meeting in the field of Boaz shows providence at work in ordinary life and introduces the kinsman-redeemer.
The threshing-floor scene is the book's turning point, where Ruth asks Boaz to act as redeemer and he promises to do so.
The legal hearing at the gate, the birth of Obed, and the genealogy reveal that this family story leads to King David.
